claims.text: A physics-informed machine-learning model incorporating defect scattering and impurity descriptors will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr electrical conductivity more accurately than traditional defect-free analytical models.
The proposed model will improve accuracy for both intrinsic and 1 wt.% oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
DFT-based scattering rates and impurity-configuration effects are useful descriptors for conductivity prediction.
Defect and impurity effects are pronounced in HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K.
Thermal activation and phonon scattering become more significant in HfNbTaTiZr over 300–1200 K.
Intrinsic imperfections and oxygen impurities produce defect structures that alter carrier-scattering rates and disrupt ideal lattice periodicity.
Analytical conductivity predictions are limited by their assumption of perfect crystals.
Enhanced impurity and defect scattering reduces conductivity in the low-temperature regime.
Phonon contributions become dominant in the 300–1200 K regime.
Representing defects, impurity configurations, and temperature effects enables the model to correct conventional analytical predictions.
The proposed model will closely match experimental conductivity measurements in both specified temperature regimes.
The accuracy improvement will be particularly strong for defect- or impurity-containing samples.
Traditional analytical models neglect the temperature dependence of defect scattering and the contribution of 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model is applicable to oxygen contents around 1 wt.% and to the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K intervals.
Additional impurity phases, severe non-stoichiometry, or phase transitions outside the proposed domain may degrade model accuracy.
